item.title: Tinubu aide dismisses claims of convoy stoning
item.description: O’tega Ogra, Senior Special Assistant to President Bola Tinubu on Digital Engagement, Strategy and New Media, has disputed claims that the president’s convoy was attacked by youths following his attendance at Friday prayers at the Shagari Central Mosque in Area 1, Abuja. Tinubu had visited the mosque in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) for the Juma’at prayer on Friday. However, Dino Melaye, a chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), later shared a video showing some youths throwing stones at a convoy believed to belong to the president. In the video, which has circulated widely on social media, some of the youths were heard chanting, “Ba ma yi, ba ma so”, a Hausa expression meaning “we don’t want you; we don’t support you”. Reacting to the development, Ogra shared a separate video showing Tinubu leaving the mosque after the prayers. “Contrary to the narrative being pushed by the opposition, with videos of their alleged paid thugs at the National Mosque today, here is footage of Mr President leaving the mosque after Friday prayers this afternoon,” Ogra wrote. The footage showed Tinubu, dressed in a white outfit and black cap, waving to youths who cheered him and took photographs with their mobile phones as he made his way into his official vehicle. Ogra’s response challenged the account circulating on social media. However, the footage he shared did not independently establish whether the incident captured in Melaye’s video occurred at another location along the president’s route. The development comes amid growing concerns over political violence ahead of the 2027 general election. In a statement he personally signed on Friday, Tinubu warned politicians and their supporters against resorting to violence, saying security agencies had been authorised to deal decisively with thuggery and other anti-democratic activities. He condemned reported incidents of violence at political events across the country and urged political actors to focus their campaigns on issues affecting the welfare of Nigerians and national development. The president reiterated that violence had no place in political campaigns. The post Tinubu aide dismisses claims of convoy stoning appeared first on Vanguard News .

When officers of the Defence Intelligence College, Abuja, visited Asaba, Azinge described an intelligence network that puts the palace at the centre of community security. “Nothing happens in this kingdom I don’t get to hear within five minutes. Good or bad, it filters into the palace, so I get to know. “It is my duty and responsibility, as the ruler of Asaba, to determine where to divert such information, depending on severity and the agency best suited to handle the issue at hand.” The system, he said, depends on trust, “We have cultivated confidence from those who provide such intelligence. item.title: Why 16 Nigerians died transiting through Addis Ababa
item.description: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja The Federal Government has advised Nigerians, particularly those with underlying health conditions, to exercise caution when travelling through Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, following the death of 16 Nigerians in the city this year. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued the advisory on Friday, revealing that Nigeria’s diplomatic mission in Addis Ababa recorded 16 deaths involving Nigerians transiting through the Ethiopian capital. The deaths were reportedly linked to health complications associated with the city’s high altitude. According to the ministry, Addis Ababa is located about 2,355 metres (7,726 feet) above sea level, where lower atmospheric pressure results in reduced oxygen levels. The ministry noted that while most healthy individuals can adapt to such conditions, travellers with pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory illnesses may face increased health risks. “This year, Nigeria’s Diplomatic Mission in Addis Ababa has recorded 16 deaths involving Nigerians transiting through the city, reportedly linked to health complications associated with high altitude,” the statement said. The government therefore urged Nigerians whose medical conditions could be worsened by high-altitude environments to seek medical advice before travelling through Addis Ababa. “Travellers with underlying medical conditions are strongly advised to obtain appropriate medical guidance before undertaking such journeys,” the ministry stated However, the Federal Government stressed that the advisory was not intended to discourage Nigerians from travelling to or transiting through Addis Ababa. “Rather, it aims to ensure that persons who may be medically vulnerable to the physiological effects of high altitudes are adequately informed and encouraged to take necessary precautions,” the statement added. The ministry reaffirmed the government’s commitment to safeguarding the health, safety and wellbeing of Nigerians abroad through timely travel advisories and other consular support measures. item.title: Egemen Mustafa Şener on the three words he learned in a Black Sea village that still run his business
item.description: Çifteköprü is a small village in the Borçka district of Artvin, in Türkiye’s Eastern Black Sea region. It is the kind of place where the weather decides more of the week than any calendar does, where a neighbour’s word carries the same weight as a document, and where the ground gives back exactly what the work put in. It is also where Egemen Mustafa Şener learned, before he ever ran a construction site in Istanbul or a shipyard project in Montevideo, the three practices that still organise his business today. The three words, as the company itself frames them, are labor, promises, and land. From a Black Sea farm to an Istanbul construction site Şener was born in Çifteköprü in May 1968. His father worked the land, his mother came from a well-established Laz family, and the household ran on a set of unspoken rules that any rural community would recognise. Work was visible or it hadn’t happened. A spoken commitment was binding. The land did not reward shortcuts. When he moved to Istanbul after high school, into business school and then into agricultural trading in the late 1980s, those rules didn’t get left behind. By the early 1990s, when he had shifted into residential and commercial construction and was managing his first sites in the city, the same three practices were doing the actual work of running the business. The language of the construction industry was new, but the habits underneath it were the same ones he had grown up with. Egemen Mustafa Şener on labor, in a sector where everything has to be seen The first of the three is labor, and in construction it is not a metaphor. Every person on a site contributes something that is either visible in the finished work or hidden inside it. A good site manager is one who can see the work that is supposed to be hidden as clearly as the work on the surface. Visible labor is also what makes delivery possible. A project is a stack of promises about what will happen on which date, and every one of those promises rests on someone actually doing the work. When labor becomes abstract, delivery slips. In three decades of residential, commercial, industrial and infrastructure projects, this has not changed. The promise that does the work before the contract does The second word is promises. item.title: Lumumba identifies what’s fueling xenophobia
item.description: •Says Africa cannot fight poverty by turning against fellow Africans Professor Patrick Loch Otieno (PLO) Lumumba has warned that Africa’s failure to create sufficient economic opportunities is fuelling xenophobia. He urged governments to address unemployment, poverty and weak industrial development rather than blame migrants for the continent’s challenges. Lumumba, a renowned Kenyan legal scholar and public speaker, said xenophobia often thrived in societies experiencing economic hardship, where unemployment, inequality and pressure on public services encouraged citizens to regard foreigners as competitors. He spoke as the keynote speaker at the Bridge Club’s grand end-of-year event in Lagos on Thursday. In his address, titled Africa Must Not Become Foreign to Itself: Xenophobia, Pan-Africanism and the Future of African Belonging, Lumumba argued that migrants were frequently made scapegoats for economic problems arising from poor governance and weak institutions. He said: “The foreign trader, worker or entrepreneur can be arrested. The failure to create productive employment over several decades cannot be arrested at a roadblock.” According to him, African governments must look beyond the presence of migrants and examine the structural weaknesses responsible for unemployment, poverty and economic competition. item.title: 2027: Violence threatens turnout as party supporters come under attacks
item.description: •60 to 70 per cent of voters afraid of voting – security analyst •INEC warns of N10m fine, jail term for inflammatory campaigns •Attacks on rallies, convoys heighten fears By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Between 60 to 70 per cent of Nigerian voters are afraid that political violence will stop them from voting in 2027, a security expert, Mr Onyekachi Adekoya, has said, as voter apathy continues to rise. Adekoya spoke on Friday morning on The Morning Brief, a programme on Channels Television. He cited a calculation by Yiaga Africa. “If you look at Yiaga Africa’s calculation, 60 to 70% of voters are worried that political violence will not allow them come out on the day,” he said. He said that fear works against turnout. “Once the violence and the rhetoric of it goes up, people are less likely to come out to vote, and perhaps that is, some would argue, part of the strategy at play by some parties,” he said. There have been recent incidents, including attacks on party convoys and on an assembly in some states including Delta, Cross River, Lagos, Edo and Gombe states. In Delta State, a man was apprehended and not handed over to the police. He was then reportedly killed. Adekoya said violence was already rising and would get worse. “It is already ticking over 70 incidents captured so far,” he said. “This is not the peak of it because the campaign season has just started.” He said the stakes went beyond 2027, with politicians positioning for 2031 and 2039. “We expect that this political season will be a bit more violent and true to type,” he said. He said pressure on local politicians would raise tensions. “Politicians at the local level are under significant pressure to deliver on their areas and that would most likely raise tensions. What it will look like is that politicians use violence to destabilize the opponents in opponents’ area of strength so that they can lose votes.” Adekoya said his firm’s report classed 14 states as toss-up states, which would be “keenly contested”. He named the North Central, North East and North West, and parts of the South East, as areas of concern. “Nobody should die because somebody is trying to be president,” he said. On what security agencies could do, Adekoya said the shortfall lay in resources. “If at all there is a failure in security it is because of lack of capacity, poor logistics planning and the fact that we have a hydraheaded security problem which cannot be resolved,” he said. He said enforcement could not be left to the agencies alone. “There is a command structure where also politics get in the way of enforcement. item.content:encoded: •60 to 70 per cent of voters afraid of voting – security analyst •INEC warns of N10m fine, jail term for inflammatory campaigns •Attacks on rallies, convoys heighten fears By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Between 60 to 70 per cent of Nigerian voters are afraid that political violence will stop them from voting in 2027, a security expert, Mr Onyekachi Adekoya, has said, as voter apathy continues to rise. Adekoya spoke on Friday morning on The Morning Brief, a programme on Channels Television. He cited a calculation by Yiaga Africa. “If you look at Yiaga Africa’s calculation, 60 to 70% of voters are worried that political violence will not allow them come out on the day,” he said. He said that fear works against turnout. “Once the violence and the rhetoric of it goes up, people are less likely to come out to vote, and perhaps that is, some would argue, part of the strategy at play by some parties,” he said. There have been recent incidents, including attacks on party convoys and on an assembly in some states including Delta, Cross River, Lagos, Edo and Gombe states. In Delta State, a man was apprehended and not handed over to the police. He was then reportedly killed. Adekoya said violence was already rising and would get worse. “It is already ticking over 70 incidents captured so far,” he said. “This is not the peak of it because the campaign season has just started.” He said the stakes went beyond 2027, with politicians positioning for 2031 and 2039. “We expect that this political season will be a bit more violent and true to type,” he said. He said pressure on local politicians would raise tensions. “Politicians at the local level are under significant pressure to deliver on their areas and that would most likely raise tensions. What it will look like is that politicians use violence to destabilize the opponents in opponents’ area of strength so that they can lose votes.” Adekoya said his firm’s report classed 14 states as toss-up states, which would be “keenly contested”. He named the North Central, North East and North West, and parts of the South East, as areas of concern. “Nobody should die because somebody is trying to be president,” he said. On what security agencies could do, Adekoya said the shortfall lay in resources. “If at all there is a failure in security it is because of lack of capacity, poor logistics planning and the fact that we have a hydraheaded security problem which cannot be resolved,” he said. He said enforcement could not be left to the agencies alone. “There is a command structure where also politics get in the way of enforcement. It should not be a job only for the police, it should be a collective responsibility,” he said. The concerns followed a run of threats by office holders in several states in recent weeks, which has drawn condemnation from civil society groups, rights organisations and opposition politicians. In Osun State, Senator Francis Adenigba Fadahunsi (Osun East) was questioned by the Nigeria Police Force over a viral video. He was heard telling supporters in Ilesa: “Until the day of election, when you see any Accord party member here in Ilesa, kill them.” Governor Ademola Adeleke rejected the senator’s clarification, called the remarks a national security threat and demanded his arrest. In the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), the Chairman of Kuje Area Council, Mr Samuel Danjuma Shekwolo, warned residents who do not support his party to relocate ahead of 2027. Amnesty International Nigeria condemned the remarks as a “call to violence.” In Borno State, the Commissioner for Youth and Sports Development, Mr Sainna Buba, said those who refuse to support the ruling party in 2027 “will be flogged.” He also warned that anyone who crossed the party would have a finger broken. In Kebbi State, the Chairman of Gwandu Local Government Area, Alhaji Atiku Ahmad Mandiya, told supporters that anyone who spoke against Governor Nasir Idris “should be dealt with.” The International Republican Institute (IRI) said civil society monitors recorded more than 81 election-related violent incidents in Osun State alone in the year before the August governorship poll. A Pre-Election Security Risk Assessment by the Kimpact Development Initiative (KDI) documented 73 election-related violent incidents, with 29 deaths, ahead of local polls in the state. Against this backdrop, the Independent National Electoral Commission INEC has warned that politicians and parties who use abusive, intemperate or inflammatory language risk fines and imprisonment under the Electoral Act 2026. INEC’s Chief Press Secretary/Media Adviser to the Chairman, Mr Adedayo Oketola, said campaign rhetoric becomes punishable once it moves beyond policy critique. “Under the Nigerian legal framework, rhetoric becomes punishable intimidation when it incites ethnic, religious, or regional hostility through abusive, base, or slanderous language explicitly designed to provoke violent emotions or target specific groups,” Oketola said, citing Section 96 of the Act. Quoting the law and attendant penalties, he said: “A political campaign or slogan shall not be tainted with abusive language directly or indirectly likely to injure religious, ethnic, tribal or sectional feelings. Any candidate who commits these offences is liable upon conviction to a maximum fine of ₦5,000,000 or imprisonment for a term of 12 months. “A non-compliant political party is liable to a fine of ₦10,000,000 in the first instance, and ₦2,000,000 for each subsequent offence.” Oketola said INEC is an election management body, not a security agency. “The Commission can issue formal queries and sanction non-compliant parties within its administrative limits,” he said. He said the Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies have a duty to prevent a breakdown of law and order, while the media and traditional and religious leaders should discourage inflammatory language. “Political campaigns should be platforms of competing ideas, not theatres of war,” Oketola said. He consequently described the purported resignation letter as fictitious or fabricated and rejected it as reliable evidence that Gombe had voluntarily vacated his office. The finding removed a central pillar of the defendants’ argument that Gombe had ceased to be an officer of the party before the July 2025 transition. Importantly, this was a finding made in determining the civil dispute, not a criminal conviction for forgery. NEC’s powers could not override the law The second major issue concerned the extent of NEC’s authority under Article 19(14) of the ADC constitution. The defendants maintained that the provision empowered NEC to dissolve the existing National Working Committee (NWC), make administrative arrangements and install the new executives. Justice Lifu acknowledged that political parties enjoy autonomy in managing their internal affairs However, he held that such autonomy must operate within the limits of the Constitution and applicable electoral legislation. He relied on Section 223(1)(a) of the 1999 Constitution, which requires political parties to provide for periodic democratic elections of their principal officers and executive committees. He also considered Sections 82(1) and 82(3) of the Electoral Act 2022, alongside the relevant provisions of the Regulations and Guidelines for Political Parties, 2022. His reasoning was that although NEC could exercise administrative powers under the party constitution, those powers could not be interpreted to dispense with mandatory democratic procedures. In effect, the authority to administer a political party was not an unrestricted licence to appoint its national executives in place of a legally required election. Emergence if new Excos The decisive weakness in the defendants’ case, according to the judge, was the absence of satisfactory evidence that the new executives emerged through a democratic electoral process. The defendants relied on documents showing that INEC had received notice of the NEC meeting, monitored its proceedings and subsequently recognised the resulting leadership. But Justice Lifu drew a clear distinction between notifying INEC and conducting a democratic election. He held that the Commission’s monitoring of the meeting did not establish that party members or duly elected delegates were given the opportunity to participate and vote for candidates of their choice. The judge explained that notice to INEC and compliance with democratic election requirements were separate legal obligations. Consequently, neither the Commission’s attendance nor its subsequent recognition could validate a process that had not been shown to comply with the law. The court therefore found no satisfactory evidence that the emergence of Mark and the other executives was preceded by, or resulted from, a democratic election as required by Section 82(3) of the Electoral Act. This was central to the outcome: the defendants could not establish the legality of their emergence merely by demonstrating that INEC had been notified of, and monitored, the NEC meeting. Internal-party-affairs argument The defendants also challenged the court’s jurisdiction, arguing that the dispute concerned the internal affairs of a political party and was therefore unsuitable for judicial intervention. Justice Lifu rejected that position Relying on the Supreme Court’s decision in Peoples Democratic Party v. Sule Lamido & Ors., he reasoned that although courts should ordinarily avoid interfering in internal political preferences, they cannot stand aside when a party’s actions are alleged to violate express constitutional or statutory provisions. He also rejected the argument that Gombe had to exhaust the party’s internal dispute-resolution mechanisms before approaching the court. The judge held that the objection was insufficient in the circumstances because the dispute raised questions of compliance with constitutional and statutory obligations. The court was therefore entitled to determine whether the leadership transition complied with the law. What the judge finally ordered Having resolved the substantive issues in Gombe’s favour, Justice Lifu invalidated the emergence of Mark and the other disputed executives, nullified the resolutions of the ADC’s 99th NEC meeting of July 29, 2025, and restrained the affected executives from presenting themselves as officers of the party. He also declared Gombe the only elected NWC member whose four-year tenure remained in force and who was legally entitled to supervise the party’s affairs. However, the judge expressly distinguished this entitlement from automatic succession to the office of National Chairman. That distinction is important. The judgment did not automatically install Gombe as National Chairman; rather, it affirmed his continuing status as the elected NWC member whose tenure remained valid and recognised his legal entitlement to supervise the party’s affairs. Ultimately, Gombe succeeded because the court found that his purported resignation had not been established, NEC’s administrative powers could not override constitutional and statutory requirements, and the Mark-led executives had failed to demonstrate that their emergence followed the legally prescribed democratic process. The central message of Justice Lifu’s decision was that a political party cannot use its internal constitution to circumvent the Constitution of the country. The ceremony took place at the Sefako M. Makgatho Presidential Guest House in Tshwane, Gauteng, and was streamed on the South African presidency’s YouTube channel. The broadcast appeared to experience a technical interruption while French Ambassador to South Africa, Antoine Michon, was speaking. Fani-Kayode was scheduled to speak next, but the livestream cut to Ramaphosa’s address to the assembled diplomats. Speaking to Vanguard, General Secretary of the Aviation Safety Round Table Initiative, ART, Mr Olumide Ohunayo, expressed concern that months after the Asaba incident, the authorities had yet to provide a comprehensive account of the investigation and the actions taken. “The DSS stepped in, the Ministry of Aviation, the NCAA, even the accident investigation body, yet nobody has come to tell us what they have done. Yes, there was a preliminary report, but I think we want to know what happened to that pilot. Are they not supposed to prosecute the pilot? What about the organisation that managed that aircraft? “I don’t think we should panic (both incidents). There is no red flag as far as I am concerned. There is this distinction between private and commercial operations. Yes, worldwide, commercial operations are stricter. There are more levels and layers of safety and certification that are compulsory before you can fly, compared to private operations. I think these incidents, which are also serious incidents, are meant to strengthen the regulations and processes in place.” Also speaking, aviation security expert, Group Captain John Ojikutu, retd, questioned the enforcement of regulations governing foreign-registered private aircraft operating in the country. He said: “How many of those aircraft are Nigerian-registered? They are all foreign-registered. What is the enforcement of regulation on them? One big man will get the aircraft, and the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority, NCAA, will not want to get too involved because of the big man or whoever has it, or if the person has contact with the political officeholders. “After the Asaba incident, what has been the report? The regulation says they (charter operators) must have security clearance. But why are they flying from one airport to the other? Are they commercial services? If it has to move from one place to another airport, it needs a security clearance. And that security clearance must be attached to the flight plan before the Air Traffic Controller, ATC, can clear. “Look at the one that claimed it was going to Asaba, but didn’t go to Asaba and dropped people. The aircraft’s ladder was down, so what did it do with the ladder? Those are the things that should concern the security agencies. That is also the concern of the NCAA.” Meanwhile, former Rector of the Nigerian College of Aviation Technology, NCAT, Capt Sam Caulcrick, said private jets had historically faced a different level of regulatory scrutiny from commercial airlines because of the distinction between the two categories of aviation. He identified the regulatory framework and funding structure of aviation agencies as factors behind the difference in oversight. According to him, commercial airlines were subject to stricter requirements because they transport fare-paying passengers, who depend on operators and regulators to ensure that aircraft maintenance and pilot qualifications meet prescribed standards. Caulcrick, however, noted that the NCAA had increased scrutiny of private jet operations, including the examination of passenger manifests to determine whether aircraft approved for non-commercial use were being deployed for charter services. He said: “Historically, private jet operations have faced less intensive regulatory oversight than commercial airlines. A primary structural driver for this difference in the aviation industry is the funding model of regulatory bodies like the NCAA. “Commercial airlines heavily subsidise regulatory agencies through mechanisms like the five per cent Ticket Sales Charge, TSC, and Cargo Sales Charge, CSC. item.title: US grounds all departing flights over communication failure
item.description: US aviation authorities on Friday ordered a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights following a communication failure affecting air traffic control centres, causing disruption and confusion among travellers across the country. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the order was issued after a technical problem affected communications across all Air Route Traffic Control Centres. In a statement, the agency said its technicians were investigating the problem. “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all US airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” the agency said. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.” The nationwide grounding is relatively rare, as similar restrictions in recent years have generally been limited to individual airlines and lasted a few hours or less. In January 2023, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop following an outage involving its Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which provides pilots with critical information about hazards, changes to airport facilities and other developments that could affect flight operations. The disruption lasted just under two hours and was considered at the time to be the first nationwide flight grounding since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Friday’s incident came a day after US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy formally requested $30.1 billion from Congress to upgrade and modernise the country’s air traffic control system. In a letter to lawmakers, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought described the proposed investment as essential to strengthening the nation’s aviation infrastructure. “This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure,” they wrote. The impact of the grounding was already being felt at airports, with passengers at Las Vegas airport reportedly informed by Southwest Airlines check-in staff that no flights would be taking off for 24 hours. …Canadian Affairs The post US grounds all departing flights over communication failure appeared first on Vanguard News .

But beyond the fascinating history, what struck me most was what China has done with this discovery. This is where the story becomes particularly interesting for Nigeria. China has not simply uncovered an ancient treasure and left it to gather dust; it has invested in archaeological research, conservation, restoration, museum infrastructure, visitor facilities and tourism development. The preservation work itself is remarkable. Some of the warriors originally had brightly painted surfaces, but exposure to the atmosphere caused much of the colour to deteriorate. This is why conservation experts have to work carefully to protect what remains. In other words, these people understand that preserving history requires knowledge, patience, investment and a long-term commitment. And they have turned that commitment into an extraordinary tourism opportunity. The Terracotta Warriors Museum attracted more than 10 million visitors in 2025. Think about the economic activities generated by that number of visitors: flights, hotels, restaurants, taxis, tour operators, souvenirs, local businesses and employment opportunities. The benefits do not end at the museum gates. Xi’an has built a thriving tourism economy around its ancient city walls, historical sites, museums, cultural performances, traditional architecture and cuisine. The city reported tourism revenue of about 376 billion Chinese yuan in 2024. Of course that figure represents the wider city’s tourism economy, not the earnings of the Terracotta Warriors Museum alone. But it demonstrates the enormous economic possibilities that can emerge when a city deliberately invests in its history and culture. Now, let us bring the conversation home. LUTH grapples staff shortage, amid brain drain The facility has been grappling with shortage of personnel following the emigration of medical doctors from the country in the past years. In November 2023, the House of Representatives Committee on Health hinted that the challenge of workforce was already leading to shutdown of wards at LUTH. The shutdown was attributed to a severe shortage of health workers, particularly nurses and doctors, highlighting the escalating brain drain crisis affecting the renowned institution. After an oversight visit to LUTH, the chairman of the committee, Dr Amos Magaji, expressed concern over the threat posed by the massive migration of health professionals in search of better opportunities abroad. Magaji lamented that the operational wards had to be shuttered due to the absence of health workers, leaving the hospital struggling to meet the health care needs of its numerous daily patients. He outlined a multifaceted approach to tackle the brain drain crisis, including interventions from university enrollment to the residency programme. While acknowledging that the issue won’t be resolved overnight, he assured that the committee is committed to implementing both short-term and long-term strategies to mitigate the impact. The committee chairman underscored the need to examine funding, infrastructure and working conditions for health professionals in Nigeria. He recognised the sacrifices made by health workers and pledged the committee’s dedication to ensuring affordable and accessible health care for Nigerians. “The government has spent a lot on infrastructure, and it is visible. LUTH today is not what it was four or five years ago. It is an irony. We have modernised wards, we can’t fully operate because we lack personnel,” the Chief Medical Director of LUTH, Prof Wasiu Adeyemo reportedly said during another round of visit by the committee in 2025. According to him, many health workers now prefer to take jobs in Lagos State-owned hospitals or travel abroad for better remuneration and opportunities, saying the state’s staff salary can be up to N120,000 higher than federal institutions like LUTH. The president of the Association of Resident Doctors, LUTH chapter, Dr Omogbolahan Adenuga, said industrial action began after efforts to resolve the issues failed. The ARD president stated that the doctors were demanding the immediate completion of the renovation of the hospital’s doctors’ residential quarters, payment of salaries owed to newly employed doctors due to delay in their enrolment on the Integrated Personnel and Payroll Information System, and the restoration of call duty meals. Adenuga said resident doctors had been forced to sleep in their cars and hospital lounges because the residential quarters undergoing renovation remained inaccessible for 18 months. He noted that the prolonged delay in completing the project had worsened the welfare of doctors, many of whom travel long distances to work. “Doctors are sleeping in their cars and in hospital lounges while treating patients. We need the federal government to release funds so that the Chief Medical Director can complete the renovation immediately. “The building has been locked for almost 18 months. It has not been completed because of lack of funding. We need the government to intervene urgently and give us a timeline for the completion of the project,” he said. item.description: On Saturday, November 7, Nigeria’s Flamingos edged out Asian giants Japan 2-1 in Rabat, Morocco, to lift the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. The Flamingos’ male counterparts, the Golden Eaglets—with five titles—remain the most successful team in the world at that level. The victorious Flamingos returned to Nigeria on Monday, November 9, to a rousing welcome. Yet amid the national celebrations, federal cash rewards, and Senate commendations, a familiar anxiety lingers over the future of the young players. Nigerias’ Flamingos U17 celebrating their World Cup win To ensure the 2026 Flamingos squad, and the next generation of young Nigerian athletes, don’t become cautionary tales, Nigerian football administrators must shift their focus from one-off tournament celebrations to sustainable career architecture. One of the biggest leaks in Nigerian football happens immediately after a youth tournament ends. Without a centralised database, young players return to disorganised local setups and vanish from national team radars. It is, therefore, a step in the right direction that the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has promised to preserve the core of the victorious Flamingos, with 11 players still eligible for the next U-17 competition. Meanwhile, the federation stated that others would be groomed for the U-20 national team, the Falconets, and eventually the Super Falcons. To achieve this objective, the NFF and the National Sports Commission (NSC) must maintain a strict digital registry for every youth international. Standout U-17 players should be systematically integrated into the U-20 Falconets and invited to understudy senior Super Falcons camps, ensuring a seamless developmental bridge rather than leaving their progress to chance. Furthermore, early exposure to humongous cash rewards has historically served as a major distraction for upcoming players. Sudden wealth without financial guidance easily erodes the discipline required for long-term growth. Acting on lessons from the past, the Federal Government decided to invest the Flamingos’ reward of N100 million each in government bonds to protect the teenage footballers from the pitfalls of sudden wealth and ensure their long-term financial security. According to the Chairman of the National Sports Commission (NSC), Mallam Shehu Dikko, the five-year investment is expected to yield annual returns of approximately 12 to 14 per cent while preserving the N100 million principal until maturity. He noted that the arrangement would enable the young players to support their education, training, and other legitimate needs without jeopardising their professional development. “What the President has done today (Wednesday, November 11) is unprecedented because these are young kids under 17. That savings bond comes with about 12 to 14 per cent interest annually, meaning each of them will be earning the equivalent of over N1.1 million monthly for the next five years. “That is enough to look after their education, their training and other needs. By the time the money matures, they will already be adults and can make clear decisions about what to do with their money,” said Dikko. Moreover, when youth stars return home without immediate European offers, playing in an underfunded domestic league with poor pitches and irregular salaries often stalls their momentum. Therefore, the NFF must strengthen the Nigeria Women Football League (NWFL) and the Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL). By enforcing club licensing standards,requiring proper training facilities, medical insurance, and guaranteed minimum wages, domestic clubs can serve as reliable springboards where teenagers play competitive minutes regularly before moving abroad. For most football stakeholders, it is a welcome development that the government has taken proactive steps to protect the Flamingos from the ordeal faced by many of their predecessors, who squandered the money accrued from continental and global victories without giving a second thought to tomorrow. However, while guiding the youngsters to make informed financial decisions and stay on their current trajectory, the menace of fake football agents must also be addressed. Sudden fame and financial windfalls often attract predatory agents who push teenagers into unsuitable foreign clubs purely for quick transfer commissions. Therefore, the NFF should vet and certify player intermediaries, offering mandatory legal and contract advisory services to youth internationals and their parents. Nigerian footballers like Sunday Mba, Macauley Chrisantus, and Kelechi Nwakali had their promising careers derailed by exploitative club deals, disputed transfers, and fraudulent foreign contracts. This has been the fate of both established youth internationals trapped in toxic professional contracts and immensely talented grassroots players lured abroad under false pretences. The Flamingos’ 2026 World Cup triumph proved once again that Nigeria has no shortage of world-class raw talent. However, trophies at age 17 are merely the starting line. By replacing ad-hoc rewards with structured mentorship, medical protection, credible management, and a strong domestic league, Nigeria can finally turn its youth champions into enduring global legends.

item.title: Tunde Bakare: The Preacher, The Politician And Two Divorcees, by Emmanuel Aziken
item.description: Many years ago, Pastor Tunde Bakare’s voice was particularly outstanding in the debate over the misuse of anointing oil, especially olive oil, as an effigy of the power of God. Many of us, including your correspondent, then based in Kaduna, were particularly enchanted by his one-hour Sunday evening television broadcasts on Channels Television where he blended Old Testament religious proclamations with contemporary political discourse in a manner that was both captivating and intellectually engaging. He was in the mould of Elijah, who challenged the wicked King Ahab; John the Baptist, who confronted Herod; and Jesus Christ, who fearlessly challenged the religious establishment and the political order represented by the likes of Herod, whom He described as a fox. Bakare projected the image of a preacher who was not afraid to speak truth to power, whether in the church or in government. His interventions were often forceful, his biblical references uncompromising, and his denunciations of religious excesses particularly refreshing to many who believed that the pulpit should remain a place of truth and accountability. The questions about Bakare, however, began to emerge after he joined the political fray. His association with Muhammadu Buhari during the 2011 election cycle was his first major public adventure into partisan politics. The political partnership did not produce the expected electoral outcome. item.content:encoded: Many years ago, Pastor Tunde Bakare’s voice was particularly outstanding in the debate over the misuse of anointing oil, especially olive oil, as an effigy of the power of God. Many of us, including your correspondent, then based in Kaduna, were particularly enchanted by his one-hour Sunday evening television broadcasts on Channels Television where he blended Old Testament religious proclamations with contemporary political discourse in a manner that was both captivating and intellectually engaging. He was in the mould of Elijah, who challenged the wicked King Ahab; John the Baptist, who confronted Herod; and Jesus Christ, who fearlessly challenged the religious establishment and the political order represented by the likes of Herod, whom He described as a fox. Bakare projected the image of a preacher who was not afraid to speak truth to power, whether in the church or in government. His interventions were often forceful, his biblical references uncompromising, and his denunciations of religious excesses particularly refreshing to many who believed that the pulpit should remain a place of truth and accountability. The questions about Bakare, however, began to emerge after he joined the political fray. His association with Muhammadu Buhari during the 2011 election cycle was his first major public adventure into partisan politics. The political partnership did not produce the expected electoral outcome. Some questioned his movement from the pulpit to the political podium, particularly against the backdrop of scriptural cautions about the tension between spiritual devotion and the worldly considerations that often drive political contests. His less-than-expected reaction to the killings of mostly Christian National Youth Service Corps members in the aftermath of the 2011 election would also have disappointed many who had looked up to him as a moral voice. Yet, his political journey continued. Before the 2023 presidential election, Bakare made an even more remarkable declaration: that he would become Nigeria’s 16th president. Many, including yours sincerely, took the pronouncement seriously, largely because of the regard in which he was held as a servant of God. A preacher who speaks with such certainty about the future, particularly when presenting it as a divine revelation, invites people to believe that his words are informed by something beyond personal ambition. The outcome of the APC presidential primary in June 2022 was therefore particularly instructive. Pastor Bakare scored zero votes. Since the emergence of Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu as Nigeria’s 16th president, not much has been heard from Bakare in the kind of forceful public interventions that once defined his ministry. That is until recent reports about his role in, or apparent sanction of, the marriage of two previously married individuals: former actor and pastor Jimmy Odukoya and his new wife, Moya Jasmine Daniel, who was previously married to British-Nigerian gospel music producer Mosadoluwa Adegboye, popularly known as Mosa. This second marriage by Pastor Jimmy Odukoya comes against the background of the controversy surrounding his succession to his late father’s church and ministry. His inheritance of the church has raised questions among some Christians about the character of religious leadership and whether a ministry established through spiritual calling should become a family inheritance passed down according to biological succession. For critics, the concern is not necessarily about whether a son can become a pastor after his father, but whether the church of God is being treated as a personal enterprise in which leadership is transferred along family lines. Many would be hard-pressed to imagine Apostle Peter, for instance, handing over the church entrusted to him and the other disciples to his children as a family inheritance. There has also been discomfort among some Christians over reports that Jimmy Odukoya was part of the groom’s entourage at his new wife’s first wedding to her former husband about ten years ago. The development has added another layer to the questions surrounding the circumstances of the present marriage. Divorce and remarriage remain subjects of considerable disagreement among Christians. However, the words of Jesus in Matthew 19:6 are unambiguous about the sanctity of marriage: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” In Mark 10:11–12, Jesus also warns against divorce followed by remarriage, describing it as adultery. Apostle Paul, in 1 Corinthians 7:10–11, instructs married couples not to separate and says that where separation occurs, the parties should remain unmarried or seek reconciliation. In verse 39, he further states that a married woman is bound to her husband for as long as he lives. There are, of course, different Christian interpretations of the biblical provisions, particularly concerning sexual immorality, abandonment and other exceptional circumstances. But the seriousness with which the New Testament treats marriage is hardly in doubt. More significantly, the Bible sets specific standards for those aspiring to Christian leadership. In 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6, Paul says that a bishop or elder must be “the husband of one wife.” It is against this background that Bakare’s reported role in the marriage of the two previously married individuals raises questions. How does a preacher who once spoke so forcefully about biblical purity and the integrity of Christian doctrine reconcile his apparent involvement with the remarriage of two divorcees? What biblical considerations informed his position? The troubling issue for many Christians is the apparent silence surrounding his reported involvement in the second marriage of Jimmy Odukoya and his new wife. What becomes of the message preached to divorced, separated and abandoned men and women who have chosen not to remarry because they believe the Bible places restrictions on divorce and remarriage? How does a pastor explain to such people that a position they have embraced at considerable personal cost may be treated differently when the individuals involved occupy prominent positions in the church? For a preacher whose public reputation was built partly on the courage to challenge religious excesses and insist on biblical truth, the questions deserve an answer. Bakare once commanded attention because he appeared unwilling to bend scripture to accommodate convenience. The challenge before him now is to explain how his present actions align with the convictions that once made his voice so compelling. The packaging has been so vastly improved upon that even a suspicious customer might not know the difference. So he consumes away. So the poison goes into the system, only to be treated by fake drugs when he falls sick. Nigerians destroying fellow Nigerians so deliberately, so callously for money. And when these so called businessmen throw parties, which they often do to celebrate their heist, they know how not to patronize their own products. Sometimes, I wonder how they sleep at night knowing they are killing people slowly with every fake product they push out. I wonder if the money they have and the lifestyle they lead are worth the lives they endanger? It gets even worse. If alcohol can be an indulgence of choice for adults, what about baby foods? I grew up with certain civic values; certain ingrained moral values that would make certain things difficult for me to do. These values are no longer active in the society. They have been dulled by a national lust for money and wealth. They have been dulled by the absence of decisive consequences for criminal and even anti-social behaviors. They have been dulled by a tacit acceptance of moral failures and even criminal tendencies by the society. Speaking at Chatham House on Thursday, INEC chairman Joash Amupitan said the commission would obey binding court decisions concerning Atiku’s participation. He also disclosed that INEC faces more than 300 pending cases and warned that unresolved disputes complicate election preparations. His remarks should not be presented as a new judgment removing Atiku from the race. They state INEC’s position on compliance with court orders. The ADC says it has appealed the November 5 ruling and applied for a stay of execution. The reporting reviewed for this edition does not establish that the stay has subsequently been granted. The political consequences of uncertainty are substantial. Candidates need to plan expenditure, organisers need direction and supporters need reliable information. INEC needs clarity for materials and logistics. The public deserves precise reporting through this process: what the court ordered, what has been challenged and what any subsequent order changes. Accusations, assurances and legal outcomes should remain clearly distinguished. Benue Brings the Campaign Back to Human Security Obi’s visit to Yelwata on Wednesday moved from an announced engagement to a completed one. Otu said the port would create opportunities in logistics, trade, fishing, shipping, tourism and shipbuilding, positioning Cross River as a maritime hub along the Gulf of Guinea. He added that the surveys exposed flaws in the 1903 navigational charts, which the Federal Government replaced on October 1, 2026, affirming the state’s littoral status. The governor also disclosed that selected indigenes of Cross River were undergoing specialised training for construction and operational roles, with plans for knowledge transfer. He identified the state’s three-way economic corridor, comprising the airport, seaport and Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, as a key link for cargo movement and investment. Otu invited investors in maritime and related industries to explore the opportunities offered by the project, citing the state’s one-stop investment hub and tax incentives. He also called on development partners to support efforts to build a resilient economy. In his goodwill message, the Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Gboyega Oyetola, commended Tinubu’s efforts to develop Nigeria’s maritime sector. He cited the establishment of the Ministry in 2023 and the approval of the country’s first National Policy on Marine and Blue Economy as steps taken to unlock the sector’s potential. Oyetola disclosed that revenue generated by agencies under the Ministry increased from ₦700.79 billion in 2023 to ₦1.83 trillion in 2025, attributing the growth to improved revenue assurance and the closure of leakages. He also listed the elimination of piracy in Nigerian waters, approval for the modernisation of the six legacy seaports and improved port governance through the Nigerian Ports Economic Regulatory Act among the administration’s achievements. The minister further cited Nigeria’s election to the decision-making Council of the International Maritime Organization after almost two decades, the lifting of United States Coast Guard restrictions on Nigerian-bound vessels in August 2026, and the release of the Cabotage Vessel Financing Fund to shipowners. He said fish production had also increased from 1.1 million to 1.4 million tonnes. Oyetola said the Bakassi port would improve market access and create industrial, investment and employment opportunities. Its connection to the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, he added, would strengthen its commercial viability and extend the benefits across Cross River, the South-South and the wider Nigerian economy. He pledged the Ministry’s support for the development of a modern, efficient and environmentally sustainable port, describing the project as an important step towards converting Nigeria’s maritime advantages into sustainable economic growth.
